documents.title: Customer Protection - Limiting Liability of Customers in Unauthorised Electronic Banking Transactions

sections.heading: Paragraph 6 - Zero Liability of a Customer
sections.text: A customer's entitlement to zero liability arises where the unauthorised transaction occurs in either of the following events: (a) contributory fraud, negligence or deficiency on the part of the bank (irrespective of whether or not the transaction is reported by the customer); or (b) third party breach where the deficiency lies neither with the bank nor with the customer but lies elsewhere in the system, and the customer notifies the bank of the unauthorised transaction within three working days of receiving communication from the bank about it.
clauses: 6(a) Zero liability applies where the bank itself is at fault (contributory fraud, negligence, or deficiency).
6(b) Zero liability also applies to a genuine third-party breach, PROVIDED the customer reports it within 3 working days of notification.

This is the real regulatory basis for concluding a case is genuine, reportable fraud rather than the customer's own doing: fault sits with the bank/system, not the customer, and it was reported promptly.

sections.heading: Paragraph 7(i) - Limited Liability: Customer Negligence
sections.text: In cases where the loss is due to negligence by a customer, such as where the customer has shared the payment credentials, the customer will bear the entire loss until the unauthorised transaction is reported to the bank. Any loss occurring after the reporting of the unauthorised transaction shall be borne by the bank.
clauses: 7(i) Where the customer's own negligence (e.g. sharing credentials) caused the exposure, the customer bears the loss up to the point of reporting; the bank bears loss after that point.
This is the real regulatory basis for a case that looks like the cardholder's own action or consent, not third-party fraud.

sections.heading: Paragraph 7(ii) and Table 1/Table 2 - Limited Liability: Delayed Reporting of a Third-Party Breach
sections.text: Where the unauthorised transaction is due to a third-party breach (fault lies neither with the bank nor the customer) and the customer reports it between 4 and 7 working days of receiving communication, the customer's liability is capped at the transaction value or a per-account-type amount set out in the circular's Table 1 (amounts vary by account/instrument type), whichever is lower. Beyond 7 working days, customer liability is determined as per the bank's Board-approved policy.
clauses: Reported within 3 working days: zero liability (see para-6-zero-liability).
Reported in 4-7 working days: capped liability per Table 1.
Reported beyond 7 working days: bank's own Board-approved policy applies, not a fixed statutory cap.
This is the real regulatory basis for treating the SPEED of a dispute report as materially relevant to the outcome, not just the fact that a dispute exists.

documents.title: UPI Unified Dispute and Issue Resolution (UDIR) - Person-to-Merchant Complaint Handling

sections.heading: P2M Complaint Response Window and Auto-Chargeback
sections.text: For person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI transactions, a complaint raised through UDIR is first routed to the merchant/beneficiary bank for investigation and response. If there is no response from the beneficiary bank or merchant within 3 days of the transaction date, the complaint is automatically converted into a chargeback against the merchant.
clauses: A merchant has a real, narrow window (3 days from the transaction date) to respond to a P2M UPI complaint before NPCI's system auto-converts it to a chargeback.

This is the real operational basis for treating dispute response as time-boxed and consequential -- a merchant that does not respond in time loses the case by default, independent of the underlying facts.

NPCI's specific internal reason-code taxonomy and evidence-submission schema for UDIR are not published publicly (comparable to FIU-IND's gated Lookup Master codes in the AML system this pipeline was adapted from) -- this pipeline uses an original, clearly-labelled POC schema for that layer (see DisputeEvidencePacket_POC.xsd) rather than inventing a fake citation for the unpublished parts.

documents.title: NPCI/UPI/OC No. 208C/2026-27 - Addendum to OC 208, 208A & 208B: Implementation of NRP & PRD Process & Arbitration Guidelines

sections.heading: Real NPCI Dispute Stage Taxonomy and Adjustment Flags (Annexure-2)
sections.text: NPCI's UPI dispute lifecycle (URCS) uses a defined sequence of stages, each with its own adjustment flag: Chargeback Raise (B), Deferred Chargeback Raise (FB), Re-presentment Raise (R), Deferred Re-presentment Raise (FR), Pre-Arbitration Raise (P), Deferred Pre-Arbitration Raise (FP), Pre-Arbitration Declined (PR), Deferred Pre-Arbitration Declined (FPR), Arbitration Raise (AR), Deferred Arbitration Raise (FAR), Arbitration Continuation (ACC), Fraud Chargeback Raise (FC), Fraud Chargeback Representment (FCR), Wrong Credit Chargeback Raise (WC), Wrong Credit Representment (WR). Critically, 'Fraud Chargeback' (FC) is a DISTINCT, separately-flagged dispute type from an ordinary 'Chargeback Raise' (B) in NPCI's own system -- this is the real operational basis for treating true_fraud and friendly_fraud/consumer-dispute as genuinely different categories, not a distinction this pipeline invented.
clauses: FC (Fraud Chargeback) is NPCI's own real, separately-tracked category for fraud-motivated disputes, distinct from an ordinary Chargeback Raise (B) -- direct operational support for scoring/routing fraud-flagged cases differently from consumer disputes.
WC (Wrong Credit Chargeback) is a further distinct category for misdirected-funds disputes, separate from both.
This is a real taxonomy from NPCI's own dispute system, not an invented category scheme.

sections.heading: Real TAT Rules for Evidence and Pre-Arbitration (Point 4, Annexure-1)
sections.text: The remitting (issuing) bank may raise a Pre-Arbitration only after the expiry of A+2 working days (A = dispute raised date), provided the beneficiary (merchant/acquiring) bank has not uploaded any evidence, or has uploaded invalid/illegible/incorrect evidence. The beneficiary bank must mandatorily upload all supporting valid evidence within A+1 working day for the re-presentment of a chargeback or pre-arbitration, to avoid further dispute lifecycle escalation.
clauses: Beneficiary (merchant-side) bank: A+1 working day to upload valid evidence, or the case escalates.
Remitting bank: may only escalate to Pre-Arbitration after A+2 working days AND only if evidence was missing/invalid.
This is the real, current operational basis for a time-boxed evidence response window -- not an approximated range.

sections.heading: Real Evidence Quality Requirement (Point 2.4, Annexure-1)
sections.text: Permitted evidence file formats are .pdf, .doc, .docx, .png, .jpg, .xls, .xlsx. Critically: text content in .doc, .docx, .xls, .xlsx is NOT accepted as valid evidence on its own -- these formats must contain images or proper proof/justification for rejecting the dispute, not merely typed assertions.
clauses: A bare textual claim (e.g. 'goods were delivered') is explicitly NOT sufficient evidence under NPCI's own rule -- genuine proof (e.g. a delivery-confirmation image/document) is required.
This is the real, current operational basis for why 'confirmed delivery evidence' (not just an assertion of delivery) is the signal this pipeline's C5 detector looks for.

documents.title: Master Circular on Credit Card, Debit Card and Rupee Denominated Co-branded Pre-paid Card Operations of Banks and NBFCs

sections.heading: Section 5 - Wrongful Billing
sections.text: The card issuing bank/NBFC should ensure that wrong bills are not raised and issued to customers. In case a customer protests any bill, the bank/NBFC should provide explanation and, if necessary, documentary evidence to the customer within a maximum period of sixty days, with a spirit to amicably redress the grievance.
clauses: A card-billing dispute (distinct from UPI's 3-day/A+1/A+2 windows) gives the issuer up to 60 days to substantiate a disputed bill with documentary evidence.

This is the real, card-channel-specific regulatory basis for a billing dispute on CARD_ECOM/CARD_POS transactions -- a genuinely different instrument and timeline than the UPI-specific NPCI circulars in this corpus, not a restatement of them.
Applies to a 'wrongful billing' complaint specifically -- the cardholder disputes the CHARGE ITSELF (e.g. wrong amount, a charge they don't recognise), not necessarily a claim of stolen credentials.

sections.heading: Section 8 - Redressal of Grievances
sections.text: Generally, a time limit of sixty (60) days may be given to customers for preferring their complaints/grievances. If a complainant does not get a satisfactory response from the bank/NBFC within a maximum period of thirty (30) days from the date of lodging the complaint, they may approach the Banking Ombudsman. The bank/NBFC shall be liable to compensate the complainant for loss of time, expenses, financial loss, and harassment/mental anguish where the grievance has not been redressed in time and the fault lies with the bank.
clauses: Customer has 60 days to file a card-billing complaint; the bank then has 30 days to respond before Ombudsman escalation.

Real compensation liability exists for the bank/NBFC specifically when the delay/fault is the BANK's, not the customer's -- relevant to distinguishing bank-side fault from a customer-side or merchant-side dispute.
This is a different escalation path (Banking Ombudsman) from NPCI's UDIR/URCS system -- card disputes and UPI disputes route through genuinely different real mechanisms.

sections.heading: Section 4(d) - Credit Reporting Withheld During a Pending Dispute
sections.text: Banks/NBFCs should be particularly careful in the case of cards where there are pending disputes. The disclosure/release of information, particularly about a default, should be made only after the dispute is settled as far as possible.
clauses: A cardholder should not be reported as a defaulter to credit bureaus while a genuine billing dispute on that specific charge is still pending.

This is real, separate evidence that RBI's card framework already anticipates disputes taking real time to resolve, and protects the cardholder's credit standing meanwhile -- relevant context for why a 'HOLD - human review' outcome (rather than an immediate concede) is itself a defensible, regulation-consistent state, not a failure to decide.

documents.title: Applying RBI's Liability Framework to Delivery Evidence (Operational Inference)

sections.heading: Why Delivery Confirmation Is Evidence Against a Zero-Liability Claim
sections.text: This section is NOT a citable regulation. It is this pipeline's own reasoning, connecting two real sources above. NPCI's own evidence-quality rule (npci-oc-208c-2026-dispute-lifecycle, evidence-quality-rule) already establishes that genuine proof, not a bare assertion, is required evidence in a dispute -- what this section adds is the inference that RBI's zero-liability protection (rbi-2017-18-15-customer-liability, para 6) is intended for genuine third-party breaches where the customer did not receive the transaction's benefit, so confirmed delivery evidence is relevant to whether a case fits that fact pattern or is better characterised as friendly fraud (a scenario RBI's bank-customer liability circular does not itself speak to, since it governs unauthorised-transaction liability, not merchant-cardholder billing disputes over goods received).
clauses: Confirmed delivery to the cardholder's own address is evidence the dispute does not fit RBI's zero-liability fact pattern (no third-party breach depriving the customer of the transaction's benefit).
No delivery confirmation is consistent with either a genuine third-party breach (RBI zero-liability may apply) or a merchant fulfilment failure -- it does not, by itself, indicate fraud either way.

The evidence-quality bar itself (proof vs. assertion) is real NPCI rule (see npci-oc-208c-2026-dispute-lifecycle); connecting that rule to RBI's liability framework is this pipeline's own inference, not a cited rule, and is presented to a human reviewer as such.

metadata.note: v4: added rbi-2006-07-12-credit-card-billing-disputes (RBI/2006-07/12, DBOD.FSD.BC.10/24.01.011/2006-07, Master Circular on Credit Card Operations, fetched and verified live via its real text-layer PDF on rbi.org.in). Added specifically because a random unbiased 12-case retrieval test after v3 showed every single case -- regardless of channel or trigger -- converging on the same top document (npci-oc-208c) with near-identical retrieval_match scores (six cases landed on the exact same 0.8193 to four decimal places): with only 4 narrow UPI/general-liability documents, there was nothing else for a CARD_ECOM/CARD_POS-channel query to match against, so retrieval couldn't discriminate case-to-case. This document is a genuinely different regulatory instrument (card-specific, not UPI-specific) with different real timelines (60-day wrongful-billing window, 30-day grievance response) and a distinct 'wrongful billing' concept, specifically to give card-channel cases something to differentiate against instead of always falling back to the UPI-specific circular. v3's npci-oc-208c-2026-dispute-lifecycle note remains accurate (source PDF was a scanned document with no text layer; read directly since Claude is multimodal and no OCR pipeline exists in this codebase). v2's two documents (RBI 2017 liability circular + NPCI UDIR) remain. The original corpus's PMLA Act + Rules documents were deliberately NOT re-added (real, but AML/KYC law, not chargeback law -- the exact domain mismatch this retrofit fixed). poc-evidence-inference-001 remains explicitly labelled as an internal inference layer, not a citable rule. Also, as of this version, legal_reasoning.py's prompt was tightened with a concrete rule_applicability calibration scale (0.8-1.0 only for a rule that directly decides the specific fact pattern, not merely topical adjacency) -- the corpus breadth and the scoring calibration were BOTH contributing to the earlier lack of variance, not one or the other.
